hints: Focus on the definition of redox, a change in oxidation number with one species oxidised and another reduced.
Notice that hydrolysis of nitriles and esters and neutralisation of acids only swap H+ and other groups, so oxidation numbers stay the same.
Look for the reaction that makes hydrogen gas from a reactive metal, as metal atoms going to ions and H+ going to H2 must involve electron transfer.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a redox reaction**

Redox means oxidation numbers change. One species loses electrons (oxidation, number increases) and another gains electrons (reduction, number decreases).

Rule to check:
$$\text{oxidation number change = redox}$$

**Classify the non-redox types**

Acid hydrolysis and acid-base neutralisation just move $\text{H}^+$, $\text{OH}^-$ and water around. No electrons are lost or gained by themselves.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Analyse the metal plus acid reaction**

Ethanoic acid with sodium gives a salt plus hydrogen gas. Sodium starts as $\text{Na}(0)$ and becomes $\text{Na}^+$, while $\text{H}^+$ becomes $\text{H}_2(0)$.

$$2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{H}_2$$
This is oxidation of Na and reduction of H+, so it is the redox reaction.

options.A: Acid hydrolysis of ethanenitrile to ethanoic acid and ammonium salt. Bonds to N and O are rearranged with water, but oxidation numbers of C, H, N and O do not change, so no redox.
options.B: Simple acid-base neutralisation of ethanoic acid to sodium ethanoate and water. It is just $\text{H}^+$ transfer from acid to $\text{OH}^-$, with Na+ as a spectator, so no oxidation or reduction.
options.C: Carboxylic acid with reactive metal gives salt plus hydrogen. $\text{Na}$ is oxidised from 0 to +1 and $\text{H}^+$ in the acid is reduced from +1 to 0 in $\text{H}_2$. Electron transfer occurs, so this is redox.
options.D: Acid hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate to ethanoic acid and ethanol. Water splits the ester linkage under $\text{H}^+$ catalysis, but all oxidation numbers remain the same, so no redox.
